items.title: The paper at a glance — sections, length and strategy
items.body:
Paper-I is **General Essay (Degree Standard), 150 marks, 180 minutes**, medium English or Telugu. You write **three essays of about 800 words**, exactly **one from each section**.

| Section | Themes |
|---|---|
| Section I | Current affairs |
| Section II | Socio-political / socio-economic / socio-environmental issues |
| Section III | Cultural & historical aspects / civic awareness / reflective topics |

**Areas tested:** (1) ability to compose a well-argued piece, (2) coherent, sequential expression, (3) awareness of the subject chosen.

**Marking credits:** observing essay format, grammatical correctness, and **originality of thought and expression**.

**Time strategy (~60 min per essay):** ~10 min plan (thesis + outline), ~40 min write, ~10 min review. Choose the topic you have the most *material* for, not just the most interesting one.
keyPoints: Paper-I General Essay: 150 marks, 180 minutes; three ~800-word essays, one per section.
Section I = current affairs; Section II = socio-political/economic/environmental; Section III = cultural-historical/civic/reflective.
Tested on: well-argued writing, coherent sequential expression, subject awareness.
Marks credit essay format, grammatical correctness, and originality.
Budget ~60 minutes per essay: plan, write, review; pick the topic with most material.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 syllabus — Paper-I General Essay (Contents, Areas of Testing, Marking).

items.title: The essay skeleton — introduction, body, conclusion
items.body:
Plan before you write. A strong 800-word essay usually has an introduction, **4-6 body paragraphs**, and a conclusion.

**Introduction (~100 words):** a hook (fact, question, anecdote or quotation) → brief context → a clear **thesis** stating your stand.

**Body (~600 words):** each paragraph develops ONE idea:
- **Topic sentence** — the paragraph's claim.
- **Evidence** — data, an example, a scheme/report.
- **Explanation** — how the evidence supports the claim.
- **Link** — back to the thesis / on to the next idea.

Arrange paragraphs by dimension — social, economic, political, environmental, ethical — or as problem → causes → solutions.

**Conclusion (~100 words):** synthesise the argument, restate the thesis in fresh words, and end with a **way forward** or a resonant thought. Never add a new argument here.
keyPoints: Plan a thesis + outline before writing.
Introduction (~100 words): hook + context + clear thesis.
Body (~600 words): 4-6 paragraphs, each = topic sentence → evidence → explanation → link.
Order paragraphs by dimension (social/economic/political/environmental) or problem-cause-solution.
Conclusion (~100 words): synthesise + restate thesis + way forward; no new arguments.

items.title: Building a well-argued, balanced essay
items.body:
The paper explicitly rewards a **well-argued** piece with **subject awareness**.

**Be multi-dimensional.** Examine an issue from several angles — social, economic, political, environmental, ethical, technological. A checklist mnemonic is **SPEET-E**.

**Be balanced.** Present more than one perspective. Acknowledge a counter-argument, then respond to it — this shows maturity, not weakness.

**Use concrete evidence:**
- Data / statistics (used honestly).
- Real examples and case studies.
- Government schemes, committees and reports — for AP-centric topics, cite **AP schemes and initiatives** (this demonstrates subject awareness).
- An apt quotation, briefly explained.

**Reach a reasoned stand.** After weighing the sides, take a clear position and justify it. Avoid sitting on the fence and avoid one-sided ranting.
keyPoints: Examine issues from multiple dimensions: social, political, economic, environmental, ethical, technological.
Balance the essay: acknowledge counter-arguments, then respond to them.
Support points with data, real examples, schemes/reports and apt quotations.
For AP-centric topics, cite AP schemes/initiatives to show subject awareness.
Weigh perspectives, then take a clear, reasoned stand — neither fence-sitting nor one-sided ranting.

items.title: Coherence, language and originality
items.body:
Marks are given for **coherent, sequential expression**, **grammatical correctness** and **originality**.

**Coherence:** ideas must flow in a logical order. Use connectives to signal the relation between paragraphs:
- Addition: *moreover, furthermore, besides*.
- Contrast: *however, in contrast, on the other hand*.
- Cause/result: *therefore, as a result, consequently*.
- Sequence: *first, next, finally*.

**Language:** prefer clear, correct sentences over ornate ones. Vary sentence length. Keep tenses consistent. Avoid slang, SMS spellings and needless jargon.

**Originality:** frame the topic in your own way, use fresh examples, and add an original insight or a local (AP) angle. Do not reproduce a memorised template word for word — examiners reward independent thought.

**Presentation:** legible handwriting, clear paragraphing, and an occasional apt sub-heading (where allowed) all help.
keyPoints: Coherence: order ideas logically and connect paragraphs with the right connectives.
Use connective families: addition, contrast, cause/result, sequence.
Language: clear correct sentences, varied length, consistent tense; avoid slang and jargon.
Originality: fresh framing, fresh examples, an original or local (AP) insight.
Do not reproduce a memorised template verbatim; presentation and paragraphing matter.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 Paper-I General Essay (coherence, grammar, originality).

items.title: Logical fallacies and common mistakes to avoid
items.body:
A well-argued essay avoids faulty reasoning.

**Common logical fallacies:**

| Fallacy | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Ad hominem | attacks the person, not the argument | 'He is rich, so his view is wrong.' |
| Hasty generalisation | concludes from too few cases | 'Two schemes failed, so all schemes fail.' |
| Slippery slope | assumes one step leads to an extreme | 'Allow this, and chaos follows.' |
| Either/or | offers only two options when more exist | 'Either ban it or accept all harm.' |
| Appeal to emotion | uses feeling instead of reason | pure sentiment, no evidence |

**Common essay mistakes:**
- No clear thesis; the essay drifts.
- A 'data dump' with no argument.
- One-sided treatment of a debatable issue.
- Repetition and padding to reach length.
- A new argument sprung in the conclusion.
- Poor time management — one essay left unfinished.
keyPoints: Avoid ad hominem: address the argument, not the person.
Avoid hasty generalisation, slippery slope, false either/or and appeal to emotion.
Always state a clear thesis; do not drift or merely dump data.
Treat debatable issues from more than one side; cut repetition and padding.
Never introduce a new argument in the conclusion; manage time so all three essays are finished.
